newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal glut signals old ways under pressure.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal glut signals old ways under pressure.

text.p: From allegations of corporate payoffs to racketeers to charges of a pension fraud scheme by a sitting member of parliament, scandals are grabbing Japan's headlines with monotonous regularity these days.

But the glut of high-profile misdeeds may signal less a rise in wrongdoing than growing intolerance for the shady practices of the past, now seen as endangering Japan's success in the global marketplace.
"These back room deals and cosy relationships built up over the postwar period. That was the way to do business -- it used to be 'Business 101' (the basics) in Japan," said a senior research analyst.
"Now the old order is breaking down. This sort of behaviour is starting to be viewed as an impediment to the modernisation and globalisation of the Japanese economy," he said.
The litany of scandals seems almost endless.

On Tuesday, prosecutors and officials of the nation's securities watchdog raided Nomura Securities Co Ltd in a sign of a deepening probe into the top brokerage's part in payments to a client linked to "sokaiya" racketeers.
The scandal -- the second to hit the brokerage in six years -- has already cost former president Hideo Sakamaki his job and threatens to dent Nomura's profits as well as damage its pride.
The Japanese public has also been treated to a steady diet of revelations in an AIDS scandal involving a government cover-up and unethical ties between companies and bureaucrats.

Nearly 400 haemophiliacs treated with unheated blood in the 1980s have contracted AIDS and activists say about 2,000 are HIV-infected as a result of professional negligence by drug makers and government officials.
On the political front, opposition legislator Tatsuo Tomobe was indicted last month on suspicion of fraud in connection with his family-run investment society.

Tomobe and the managers of the society, Orange Kyosai Kumiai, are accused of defrauding depositors of millions of yen with promises of high interest payments. Japanese media said he spent one billion yen ($8 million) to win party endorsement as a candidate in a 1995 Upper House election, which he won.

That scandals involving practices long known to have gone on behind closed doors are hitting the front pages daily suggests a subtle shift in attitudes of a public grown less tolerant of corruption, some analysts said.

"I think that the cost of corruption is higher now than it used to be when the economy was growing very strongly," said one foreign economist. "Structurally bred corruption is not efficient...and the environment is much harsher so there is less tolerance both from voters and from customers."

Japan's economy has struggled for much of this decade to cope with fallout from the collapse of the late 1980s "bubble" of exhorbitant land and share prices, and while growth was a solid 3.6 percent in 1996, worries about the future remain.

Moves to cut through the web of regulations woven into Japan's economic fabric could in the end make corruption involving corporate payoffs to bureaucrats and politicians less attractive. And efforts to free up Tokyo's financial markets and make its financial firms more competitive globally will increase pressure for stricter corporate ethics, analysts say.

Ironically, the steady stream of scandals could itself give greater impetus to deregulation efforts, attempts which thus far have often been scuttled or watered down by special interests opposed to reform.

"We have found with scandals that this has led to an undermining of confidence in bureaucrats, which has led to more calls for change in Japan," Larry Greenwood, economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo, said recently.

Changes in business and political ethics, however, are almost certain to occur at a measured pace. "It's like everything else here -- you can't wake up one day and just eradicate what has become time-honoured tradition," the analyst said. ($1=124 yen)
